name: VitaCore LinguaSync Real-Time Translation Implant
body_location: cranial — auditory cortex interface with subdermal mastoid processor
description:
The LinguaSync is a real-time spoken language translation system delivered as a cranial implant, interfacing directly with the auditory processing cortex and a subdermal signal processor housed behind the mastoid bone. When the wearer hears speech in a language flagged as non-primary in their profile, the system intercepts the auditory signal before conscious processing, applies neural translation encoding drawn from VitaCore's continuously updated PolyNet language model, and delivers the translated meaning as a secondary auditory layer — experienced not as a separate voice, but as a seamless overlay, as if the speaker had always been speaking the user's preferred language. The current LinguaSync ships with 94 active language profiles and 31 regional dialect packs, with additional language packs purchasable via subscription. It does not produce spoken output; it is a comprehension tool, not a speaking aid.

GLMZ is a city of layered migrations, and the LinguaSync is as essential to daily life as transit cards. On the Shelf, where communities from Lagos, Guangzhou, Kraków, and Bogotá exist in the same block — often in the same building — the ability to understand your neighbors, your landlord, your employer, and the city's bureaucratic systems without spending years in language acquisition is not a luxury but a survival tool. Tier 2 workers use it to navigate corporate environments where Mandarin, English, and Portuguese shift mid-meeting without acknowledgment. Children who immigrated young often have it installed alongside their first school implants. The experience of the city changes fundamentally with a LinguaSync — walls come down, misunderstandings collapse, and the texture of overheard conversation becomes rich in a way that monolingual life never offers.
installation_requirements: Outpatient clinic or licensed pharmacy; 60-minute procedure; local anesthetic; same-day discharge
maintenance: Language model updates pushed automatically via PolyNet subscription (Φ8/month or Φ80/year); annual hardware check recommended; processor rated for 10-year service life

side_effects: Translation shimmer during rapid multilingual switching — a half-second lag where both languages are briefly perceived simultaneously
Occasional phantom speech — the auditory overlay triggering faintly during silence or white noise in the first calibration month
Some users report that their native language begins to feel 'louder' than translated speech, a perceptual imbalance that typically resolves within six weeks
Mild headache and jaw tension in the first week post-installation due to processor housing adjustment
cultural_context: The LinguaSync occupies an interesting cultural position in GLMZ: it is ubiquitous enough to be unremarkable in most contexts, yet its absence is immediately noticeable. In diverse neighborhoods, not having one marks you either as someone very new to the city, someone ideologically opposed to implants, or someone who has lived so insularly that they've never needed one. There is a generational divide in how the implant is perceived: older residents who learned languages the hard way sometimes regard it with mild contempt, feeling that it produces a kind of cultural laziness — understanding without effort, comprehension without relationship. Younger residents find this argument incomprehensible, the equivalent of complaining that calculators make people bad at arithmetic. A small community of professional translators and interpreters maintains that the LinguaSync flattens nuance and idiomatic depth, and they are not entirely wrong — the system handles pragmatic meaning well, but poetry, humor, and cultural subtext remain areas of ongoing improvement.

story_hooks: A character's LinguaSync begins translating a language that isn't in VitaCore's database — something that sounds constructed, consistent, and deliberate, spoken by individuals who clearly don't want to be understood.

The PolyNet subscription model means VitaCore technically processes all intercepted speech through its servers for model training — a privacy clause buried in the EULA that someone has just figured out how to exploit.
A community that has deliberately developed a creole dialect specifically to defeat LinguaSync translation hires the party to keep it that way when VitaCore announces a new dialect pack.
